title: Blockchain & Cryptocurrency Laws and Regulations 2025/BATTLE FOR THE PLANET OF THE BORED APES: REGULATION OF DIGITAL ASSETS
content:
BLOCKCHAIN & CRYPTOCURRENCY LAWS AND REGULATIONS 2025
BATTLE FOR THE PLANET OF THE BORED APES: REGULATION OF DIGITAL ASSETS
FREE ONLINE ACCESS
CHAPTER CONTENT
Background
Non-fungible tokens
Digital assets as securities
Regulation of digital asset platforms
SEC enforcement actions against issuers of digital assets
Mann and Frye v. SEC
Private plaintiff actions against issuers of NFTs
Petition for rulemaking
Rulemaking and the APA
Conclusion
Like the violent struggle to coexist between the great apes and humans in the Planet of the Apes movies,[i] the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) and the creators of digital assets and non-fungible tokens (“NFTs”) appear to be mired in a similar existential contest.  The struggle between the SEC and the creators of digital assets dates back to 2013 and the SEC action against Trendon Shavers.[ii]  More recently, in October 2022, Bloomberg reported that the SEC was investigating Yuga Labs – the creator of the Bored Ape Yacht Club NFT collection – over whether sales of its digital assets[iii] violate federal securities laws.[iv]  The investigation was focused on whether Yuga’s NFTs are securities and how ApeCoins, the Ethereum-based governance and utility tokens used within the APE ecosystem, were distributed to holders of Bored Ape Yacht Club, Mutant Ape Yacht Club, and Bored Ape Kennel Club members.  The investigation of Bored Ape and other issuers of NFTs is another demonstration of the SEC’s view that nearly all digital assets, including NFTs, are securities.
This chapter includes: (i) an introduction to blockchain technology and digital assets; (ii) an introduction to how digital assets can be deemed securities; (iii) the use of enforcement as a means of regulating digital assets as securities; (iv) the regulation of trading platforms that facilitate the trading of digital assets that are securities; (v) a discussion of a petition for guidance on the regulation of digital assets and the platforms that facilitate the trading of digital assets; and (vi) a discussion of a regulatory approach that would be preferred by the FinTech industry – a constructive dialogue between the SEC and the FinTech industry through rulemaking that is subject to the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”).[v]
BACKGROUND
The past several years have seen a proliferation of digital assets, including NFTs.  Digital assets are intangible assets that rely on distributed ledger technology, commonly known as blockchain, and exist in a variety of forms and provide industry actors with a variety of benefits.[vi]  Cryptocurrencies and tokens are unique subsets of digital assets that utilize cryptography to assure the authenticity of digital assets by creating a secure, distributed network for transactions.[vii]
The SEC has defined digital assets as “an asset that is issued and transferred using distributed ledger or blockchain technology.”[viii]  Although a “digital asset” is not explicitly defined in U.S. securities laws, a digital asset may in certain instances be deemed a security and, in such instances, the SEC often refers to these digital assets that are securities as “digital asset securities.”[ix]
NON-FUNGIBLE TOKENS
NFTs have gained notoriety as a popular means of buying and selling digital collectibles representing tangible and intangible assets across multiple industries, including art, sports, music, fashion, and gaming.  Since November 2017, there has been approximately $200 million spent on purchases of NFTs, with perhaps the most famous sale occurring on March 11, 2021, when artist Mike Winkelmann, also known as Beeple, used an NFT to sell his digital art “Everydays: the First 5000 Days” for $69 million.[x]  The sale was the third-highest price paid for a piece of art by a living artist.  Four days prior to Beeple’s sale, an NFT of a video clip of LeBron James dunking a basketball sold for $208,000 on NBA Top Shot.[xi]  Meanwhile, Jack Dorsey, the creator of Twitter, auctioned his first-ever tweet as an NFT for $2.9 million.
NFTs are not just limited to digital collectibles.  One of the more exciting possibilities for NFTs lies in the creation of new markets and forms of investments whereby physical assets can be fractionalized and sold to multiple consumers.  As NFTs proliferate across multiple mediums and technologists develop new ways to deploy NFTs, particularly in the financial services sector, these innovators will inevitably run headfirst into regulators tasked with the challenge of protecting investors and maintaining safe, sound and efficient markets.  As Yuga and Bored Ape Yacht Club holders will tell you – some already have.
NFTs are not like cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, which function as the native asset of a blockchain.  NFTs are created as part of a platform built on an existing blockchain (like the Ethereum blockchain) and are not fungible like other cryptocurrencies, meaning NFTs cannot be traded or exchanged for one another without inherent diminution in value (i.e., one dollar is always worth one dollar and one Bitcoin is always equal to another Bitcoin).[xii]  Instead, NFTs are individually unique and use blockchain technology to establish authenticity, ownership and transferability of a unique asset.  An NFT is created from digital objects that represent both tangible and intangible property, including, but not limited to: (i) artwork; (ii) videos; (iii) collectibles and antiques; (iv) video game avatars; and (v) music.  When an individual buys an NFT, the purchaser can receive exclusive ownership rights to the underlying asset as well as a digital token with unique data verifying the provenance of the underlying asset.  Blockchain technology and NFTs can provide artists, athletes and celebrities a unique opportunity to leverage their fame and talent in the digital space and monetize themselves and their products.[xiii]  For example, artists can create and digitize their own content and sell it directly to consumers as an NFT and, in doing so, capture most of the revenue generated from such sale.
The utility of NFTs can go far beyond digitizing popular culture content.  NFTs also carry with them the potential to revolutionize financial services, particularly investment activities among retail investors.  For example, NFTs can be used to fractionalize certain assets, such as real estate, making the underlying real estate asset easier to divide among multiple owners.  These fractionalized NFTs can then be tradeable on an appropriate exchange platform, which introduces new investment opportunities for investors to diversify their portfolios.
DIGITAL ASSETS AS SECURITIES
The SEC evaluates digital assets in the same manner as traditional assets to determine whether they are securities.  Unlike initial coin offerings, which are a type of digital asset that has drawn a considerable level of attention from SEC staff,[xiv] NFTs have not been the subject of interpretative guidance or rulemaking by the SEC.  The SEC has initiated enforcement actions against the creators of digital assets, but has not brought an enforcement action against the operator of a platform that facilitates the offer and sale of NFTs – yet.[xv]
Absent guidance from regulators, the issue of when an NFT is considered a security by the SEC remains unclear, although we now have some guidance from the courts.
WHAT IS A SECURITY?
The definitions of “security” under the Securities Act of 1933 (“Securities Act”) and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”) are nearly identical and broad enough to cover some NFTs.  Section 2(a)(1) of the Securities Act defines a “security” as:
[A]ny note, stock, treasury stock, security future, security-based swap, bond, debenture, evidence of indebtedness, certificate of interest or participation in any profit-sharing agreement, collateral-trust certificate, preorganization certificate or subscription, transferable share, investment contract, voting-trust certificate, certificate of deposit for a security, … or, in general, any interest or instrument commonly known as a “security.”[xvi]
It was the intent of Congress to define a “security” to include the many types of instruments that in the commercial world fall within the concept of a security,[xvii] and courts have interpreted the definition of security in the federal securities laws broadly.[xviii]  The definition of “security” is sufficiently expansive to grant the SEC authority to regulate a variety of products as securities, including stocks, bonds, and notes, as well as the various collective investment pools and common enterprises devised by persons seeking to generate profits from the efforts and investments of others (i.e., investment contracts).[xix]
In determining whether an instrument is a security, courts often look at the economic reality and focus on the substance rather than form.[xx]  In enforcement actions, the SEC has argued that offerings of digital assets are investment contracts.[xxi]  While the definition of security is very broad, it does not explicitly include digital assets.  However, in certain circumstances, a digital asset could be deemed an investment contract.
HOWEY
What constitutes an investment contract is determined by the test articulated by the U.S. Supreme Court in SEC v. W.J. Howey Co.[xxii]  Under the Howey test, an investment contract is a contract, transaction, or scheme involving (i) an investment of money, (ii) in a common enterprise, (iii) with the expectation of profits that will be derived from the efforts of the promoter or a third party.  The Howey test brings many non-traditional offerings within the scope of the term “security.”
INVESTMENT OF MONEY
The SEC has taken the position that the investment does not have to be in the form of “money,” but it can be any “specific consideration in return for a separable financial interest with the characteristics of a security.”[xxiii]  The first prong of the Howey test is typically satisfied in an offer and sale of a digital asset because the digital asset is purchased or otherwise acquired in exchange for value, whether in the form of fiat currency or another digital asset as consideration.[xxiv]
COMMON ENTERPRISE
Courts have generally analyzed “common enterprise” as a distinct element of an investment contract.  However, there is a split in authority among the federal circuit courts regarding what constitutes a “common enterprise.”  The courts are divided regarding whether horizontal or vertical commonality is required (and, in the latter case, whether the broad or narrow variety is required) to satisfy the Howey common enterprise requirement.
A majority of the circuit courts require or recognize a showing of “horizontal commonality,” which involves the pooling of assets from multiple investors in such a manner that all share in the profits and risks of the enterprise.[xxv]  In horizontal commonality, the fortunes of each investor depend upon the profitability of the enterprise as a whole.
Other circuit courts, including the Ninth Circuit that includes California, have held that a “common enterprise” exists by virtue of “vertical commonality,” which focuses on the relationship between the promoter and the body of investors.[xxvi]  In this approach, an investor’s fortunes are tied to the promoter’s success rather than to the fortunes of his or her fellow investors.  This approach focuses on the community of interest between the individual investor and the manager of the enterprise.[xxvii]  In vertical commonality, the investors’ fortunes need not rise and fall together, and a pro rata sharing of profits and losses is not required.[xxviii]  It is also not necessary that the funds of investors be pooled.[xxix]
REASONABLE EXPECTATION OF PROFITS DERIVED FROM THE PROFITS OF OTHERS
Under the Howey test, profits can be either capital appreciation resulting from the development of the initial investment, or a participation in earnings resulting from the use of investors’ funds.[xxx]  Profits are income or return that investors seek on their investment, not the profits of the scheme in which they invest.[xxxi]  Profits include, for example, dividends, other periodic payments, or the increased value of the investment.  The determining factor under this prong of the Howey test is that the investor is “attracted solely by the prospects of a return” on his or her investment.[xxxii]  The investor may not have been motivated by a desire to use or consume the item purchased.[xxxiii]  In determining whether an investor was “attracted or led” by the expectation of profits, courts look at whether the promoter has induced prospective investors with proposed or promised profits.
While the SEC has not provided guidance on when an NFT is a security, the SEC staff has noted:
[T]he main issue in analyzing a digital asset under the Howey test is whether a purchaser has a reasonable expectation of profits (or other financial returns) derived from the efforts of others.  A purchaser may expect to realize a return through participating in distributions or through other methods of realizing appreciation on the asset, such as selling at a gain in a secondary market.[xxxiv]
If a digital asset relates to an existing asset and is marketed as a collectible with a public assurance of authenticity on the blockchain, it should not be deemed a security.  If a digital asset promises a return on investment from the efforts of others, the digital asset will likely be deemed a security.  However, as noted by the SEC staff in its 2019 Framework for “Investment Contract” Analysis of Digital Assets: “Price appreciation resulting solely from external market forces (such as general inflationary trends or the economy) impacting the supply and demand for an underlying asset generally is not considered ‘profit’ under the Howey test.”[xxxv]
FRACTIONALIZED NFTS
As NFTs proliferate, new regulatory questions will arise.  Fractionalized NFTs could be considered a security.  While NFTs are meant to be non-fungible, fractional NFTs that allow numerous purchasers to acquire a partial ownership interest in the NFT increases the likelihood that the NFT could be deemed a security.
REGULATION OF DIGITAL ASSET PLATFORMS
If a digital asset is a security, the platform facilitating the sale and secondary trading of the digital asset may have to register with the SEC as an exchange or a broker-dealer and alternative trading system (“ATS”).
SECURITIES EXCHANGE
Section 3(a)(1) of the Exchange Act defines an “exchange” as “any organization, association, or group of persons, whether incorporated or unincorporated, which constitutes, maintains, or provides a market place or facilities for bringing together purchasers and sellers of securities or for otherwise performing with respect to securities the functions commonly performed by a stock exchange as that term is generally understood … .”[xxxvi]  Exchange Act Rule 3b-16(a) provides a functional test to assess whether a trading system meets the definition of exchange.  Under Rule 3b-16(a), an organization, association, or group of persons will be deemed to provide “a marketplace or facilities for bringing together purchasers and sellers of securities or for otherwise performing with respect to securities the functions commonly performed by a stock exchange” if such organization, association, or group of persons: (1) brings together the orders for securities of multiple buyers and sellers; and (2) uses established, non-discretionary methods (whether by providing a trading facility or by setting rules) under which such orders interact with each other, and the buyers and sellers entering such orders agree to the terms of the trade.
As the SEC noted in the DAO Report, a system that meets the definition of an exchange and is not excluded under Rule 3b-16(b) must register as a national securities exchange or operate pursuant to an appropriate exemption.[xxxvii]  One frequently used exemption is for platforms that register with the SEC as an ATS.  Rule 3a1-1(a)(2) exempts from the definition of “exchange” under Section 3(a)(1) an ATS that complies with Regulation ATS.  An ATS that operates pursuant to the Rule 3a1-1(a)(2) exemption and complies with Regulation ATS would not be subject to the registration requirement of Section 5 of the Exchange Act.
If a digital asset is a security, any platform that brings together multiple buyers and sellers of the digital assets using non-discretionary methods will likely be deemed an exchange.
ALTERNATIVE TRADING SYSTEMS
In 1998, the SEC adopted Regulation ATS, which allows an ATS to choose whether to register as a national securities exchange or to register as a broker-dealer and comply with additional requirements of Regulation ATS.  An “alternative trading system” means any organization, association, person, group of persons, or system that: (i) constitutes, maintains, or provides a marketplace or facilities for bringing together purchasers and sellers of securities or for otherwise performing with respect to securities the functions commonly performed by a stock exchange within the meaning of Rule 3b-16 under the Exchange Act, and (ii) does not set rules governing the conduct of subscribers other than the conduct of such subscribers’ trading on such organization, association, person, group of persons, or system, or discipline subscribers other than by exclusion from trading.[xxxviii]
A digital asset platform may be required by the SEC to register as an ATS if it maintains a marketplace or facilities for bringing together purchasers and sellers of digital assets that are deemed securities, and it does not set rules governing the conduct of subscribers other than the conduct of such subscribers’ trading on such platform.  If the platform is not required to register as an ATS, the operator of the platform may be required to register as a broker-dealer.
BROKER-DEALERS
Section 15 of the Exchange Act requires registration with the SEC of all broker-dealers using interstate commerce or the facilities of any national securities exchange to effect transactions in securities (other than exempted securities and certain short-term debt instruments).  Section 3(a)(4)(A) of the Exchange Act defines a “broker” as “any person engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others.”  The Exchange Act and the rules thereunder do not define these terms.  The SEC and the courts have taken an expansive view of the scope of these terms.[xxxix]  The SEC and the courts apply a “facts and circumstances” analysis in evaluating whether a person has acted as a broker, with no single element being dispositive.[xl]
Depending on the circumstances, the operator of a digital asset platform may be deemed a broker-dealer if the operator of the platform is deemed to be engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others.
ENGAGED IN THE BUSINESS
Courts have read “engaged in the business” as connoting a certain regularity of participation in purchasing and selling activities rather than a few isolated transactions.[xli]  Two factors are important in determining whether there is “regularity of business”: the number of transactions and clients, and the dollar amount of securities sold; as well as the extent to which advertisement and investor solicitation were used.[xlii]  Besides “regularity of business,” courts and the SEC have identified several other factors that indicate that a person is “engaged in the business.”[xliii]  These factors include: (i) receiving transaction-related compensation; (ii) holding oneself out as a broker, as executing trades, or as assisting others in settling securities transactions; and (iii) soliciting securities transactions.
The operator of a digital asset platform could be deemed to be engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities because it will more than likely receive transaction-related compensation, execute trades for users of the platform, and solicit users to engage in such transactions.
“FOR THE ACCOUNT OF OTHERS”
A “broker” is a person that effects transactions in securities for others, not itself.  A firm that effects transactions solely on its own behalf should not be considered to be acting as a “broker.”[xliv]  Unless the operator of a digital asset platform is executing all transactions as a principal to the transaction, the platform operator could be deemed to be effecting transactions in securities for others.
ROLE OF COMPENSATION IN ANALYSIS
SEC guidance and enforcement actions have noted that the receipt of commissions or other transaction-related compensation is an important factor in deciding whether a person is a “broker” subject to the registration requirements under the Exchange Act.[xlv]  Transaction-related compensation refers to compensation based, directly or indirectly, on the size, value or completion of any securities transactions.  The SEC will look behind the terms of a compensation arrangement to determine its economic substance, that is, to determine whether it is transaction-related.  The receipt of transaction-based compensation often indicates that a person is engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities.[xlvi]
If the operator of a digital asset platform receives transaction-related compensation in the sale of a digital asset that is deemed a security, the platform could be deemed to be acting as a broker-dealer.
EFFECTING TRANSACTIONS IN SECURITIES
Courts and the SEC have determined that a person “effects transactions in securities” if the person participates in such transactions “at key points in the chain of distribution.”[xlvii]  Participation may include: (i) assisting an issuer to structure prospective securities transactions; (ii) helping an issuer to identify potential purchasers of securities; (iii) screening potential participants in a transaction for creditworthiness; (iv) soliciting securities transactions (including advertising); (v) negotiating between the issuer and the investor; (vi) making valuations as to the merits of an investment or giving advice; (vii) taking, routing or matching orders, or facilitating the execution of a securities transaction; (viii) handling customer funds or securities; and (ix) preparing and sending transaction confirmations (other than on behalf of a broker-dealer that executes the trades).  Handling customer funds may also include handling a customer’s digital currencies, such as Bitcoin, in connection with Bitcoin denominated securities transactions.[xlviii]
The SEC could deem a platform that is facilitating transactions in digital assets to be effecting securities transactions if it is helping an issuer to identify potential purchasers of securities.  A digital asset platform that solicits securities transactions and facilitating negotiations between the issuer and the investor could be deemed to be effecting securities transactions.  The operator of a digital asset trading platform that takes, routes, or matches orders, or facilitates the execution of a securities transaction, could be viewed as effecting transactions in securities.  Finally, the operator of a digital asset trading platform that handles customer funds (even if the funds are a digital currency) or securities could be deemed to be effecting transactions.
SEC ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS AGAINST ISSUERS OF DIGITAL ASSETS
The SEC has entered into settlements with several creators of digital assets.  While each case is fact-specific, the settlements shed light on the SEC’s views on when a digital asset will be deemed a security.
RIPPLE
On July 13, 2023, Judge Analisa Torres of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York issued a decision in the SEC’s case against Ripple Labs (“Ripple”).[xlix]  The court appeared to deliver partial victories to both the SEC and to Ripple on the parties’ summary judgment motions in perhaps the most anticipated decision to date in the digital asset industry.
The blockchain “XRP Ledger” was developed in 2011 along with 100 billion XRP tokens, which is the native digital token of the XRP Ledger and is required to perform any transactions on the XRP Ledger.  In 2012, one of the XRP Ledger’s creators founded Ripple.  Ripple’s founders retained 20 billion XRP tokens for themselves and provided the remaining 80 billion XRP tokens to Ripple.  Between 2013 and 2020, Ripple engaged in various sales and distributions of XRP: Ripple sold approximately $730 million’s worth of XRP tokens directly to third parties in private sales, including institutions and hedge funds (termed “Institutional Sales”); Ripple sold roughly $750 million’s worth of XRP tokens on digital asset exchanges using trading algorithms (termed “Programmatic Sales”); and Ripple distributed roughly $610 million’s worth of XRP as a form of payment for services (termed “Other Distributions”).  Ripple’s founders sold some or all their XRP tokens in their individual[l] capacities (e.g., one founder sold $450 million’s worth of XRP tokens).[li]
Judge Torres ruled that Ripple’s Institutional Sales of XRP to sophisticated individuals and entities pursuant to written contracts amounted to unregistered offers and sales of investment contracts in violation of Section 5 of the Securities Act.[lii]  Institutional Buyers invested money by purchasing XRP tokens, horizontal commonality existed because the fortunes of each investor were tied to other investors and to Ripple, and the Institutional Buyers purchased XRP with the expectation that they would derive profits from Ripple’s efforts.[liii]
Judge Torres concluded that Ripple’s Programmatic Sales, which were sales of XRP by Ripple to public buyers on digital asset exchanges, did not constitute offers and sales of investment contracts because the sales were blind bid/ask transactions, and the buyers would not have known if their payments were going to Ripple or another seller of XRP.[liv]  Judge Torres held that “the economic reality is that Programmatic Buyers stood in the same shoes as a secondary market purchase who did not know to whom or what it was paying its money.”[lv]  Thus, there could be no reasonable expectation that the buyers would derive profits from Ripple’s efforts vis-à-vis the funds from the XRP sale.[lvi]  Judge Torres further noted that “it is not enough for the SEC to argue that Ripple ‘explicitly targeted speculators’ or that ‘Ripple understood that people were speculating on XRP as an investment’ because a speculative motive ‘on the part of the purchaser or seller does not evidence the existence of an ‘investment contract’ within the meaning of the [Securities Act]’.”[lvii]  The court noted that someone buying a horse or a car hoping to realize a profitable investment is not buying a security because the expected return is not contingent upon the continuing efforts of someone else.[lviii]
Judge Torres held that the Programmatic Buyers may have purchased XRP with an expectation of profit, “but they did not derive that expectation from Ripple’s efforts (as opposed to other factors, such as general cryptocurrency market trends) – particularly because none of the Programmatic Buyers were aware that they were buying XRP from Ripple.”[lix]  The court explained that some Programmatic Buyers may have purchased XRP with the expectation of profits to be derived from Ripple’s efforts, but that “the inquiry is an objective one focusing on the promises and offers made to investors; it is not a search for the precise motivation of each individual participant.”[lx]  However, despite cryptocurrency exchanges’ rush to relist XRP following Judge Torres’ decision (e.g., Coinbase relisted XRP within hours), the order does not address whether secondary sales of XRP on third-party operated platforms are securities or the permissibility of cryptocurrency exchanges to facilitate the purchase and sale of XRP.[lxi]
Judge Torres concluded that Ripple’s distribution of XRP to employees and as compensation to third parties did not amount to investment contracts because those transfers of XRP were not done pursuant to an “investment of money,” as required under Howey.[lxii]  Ripple never received any payments from these XRP distributions, and therefore the distributions could not be investment contracts.[lxiii]
On July 13, 2024, Judge Torres ordered Ripple to pay the SEC $125 million in civil penalties over charges of improperly selling the cryptocurrency XRP.[lxiv]  The SEC had been seeking fines and penalties totaling $2 billion.  Judge Torres imposed the fine after finding that 1,278 institutional sale transactions by Ripple violated the Securities Act.  The $125 million fine is well below the $1 billion in disgorgement and prejudgment interest and $900 million in civil penalties the SEC sought.  The order followed the judge’s July 2023 ruling in the case finding that Ripple violated federal securities laws through its direct sale of XRP to institutional clients, though she also ruled that Ripple’s Programmatic Sales of XRP to retail clients through exchanges did not violate any securities laws.
Judge Torres also banned Ripple from future violations of federal securities laws on Wednesday, saying that while she is not making a judgment that Ripple has violated any laws after the SEC filed its lawsuit, the company may well “cross the line” in a section referring to Ripple’s “on-demand liquidity” offerings.  “Rather, the Court finds that Ripple’s willingness to push the boundaries of the Order evinces a likelihood that it will eventually (if it has not already) cross the line,” she said.  “On balance, the Court finds that there is a reasonable probability of future violations, meriting the issuance of an injunction.”[lxv]
The injunction requires Ripple to file a registration statement if it intends to sell any securities.  The SEC is likely to appeal the July 2023 ruling now that the judge has imposed a sentence, after the same judge denied the SEC’s motion for an interlocutory appeal last year.  It is unclear how Judge Torres reached her conclusion that the SEC was only entitled to a fine of $125 million when the remedy for an illegal offer and sale of securities is recission.  Consistent with Judge Torres ruling that Ripple had conducted an illegal offer and sale of a security – XRP – the penalty should have been at least the value of the primary offering of XRP (the Institutional Sales) – approximately $730 million.[lxvi]
STONER CATS
The SEC charged Stoner Cats 2 LLC (“Stoner Cats”) with conducting an unregistered offering of crypto asset securities in the form of NFTs that raised approximately $8 million from investors to finance an animated web series called Stoner Cats.[lxvii]  According to the SEC order, on July 27, 2021, Stoner Cats offered and sold to investors more than 10,000 NFTs for approximately $800 each, selling out in 35 minutes.[lxviii]  Before and after Stoner Cats NFTs were sold to the public, Stoner Cats’ marketing campaign highlighted specific benefits of owning them, including the option for owners to resell their NFTs on the secondary market.[lxix]  The Stoner Cats team emphasized its expertise as Hollywood producers, its knowledge of crypto projects, and the well-known actors involved in the web series, leading investors to expect profits because a successful web series could cause the resale value of the Stoner Cats NFTs in the secondary market to rise.[lxx]  The company configured the Stoner Cats NFTs to provide a 2.5 percent royalty for each secondary market transaction in the NFTs and encouraged individuals to buy and sell the NFTs, leading purchasers to spend more than $20 million in at least 10,000 transactions.[lxxi]
According to the SEC order, Stoner Cats violated the Securities Act by offering and selling these crypto asset securities to the public in an unregistered offering that was not exempt from registration.[lxxii]  Stoner Cats agreed to a cease-and-desist order and to pay a civil penalty of $1 million.[lxxiii]  The order establishes a Fair Fund to return monies that injured investors paid to purchase the NFTs.[lxxiv]  Stoner Cats also agreed to destroy all NFTs in its possession or control and publish notice of the order on its website and social media channels.[lxxv]
IMPACT THEORY
The SEC charged Impact Theory LLC (“Impact Theory”), a media and entertainment company headquartered in Los Angeles, with conducting an unregistered offering of crypto asset securities in the form of purported NFTs.[lxxvi]  The company raised approximately $30 million from hundreds of investors, including investors across the United States, through the offering.[lxxvii]  From October to December 2021, Impact Theory offered and sold three tiers of NFTs, known as Founder’s Keys, which Impact Theory called “Legendary,” “Heroic,” and “Relentless.”[lxxviii]  The company encouraged potential investors to view the purchase of a Founder’s Key as an investment into the business, stating that investors would profit from their purchases if Impact Theory was successful in its efforts.[lxxix]  The company emphasized that it was “trying to build the next Disney,” and, if successful, it would deliver “tremendous value” to Founder’s Key purchasers.[lxxx]  The NFTs offered and sold to investors were deemed by the SEC to be investment contracts and therefore securities.[lxxxi]  Accordingly, the SEC asserted that Impact Theory violated the federal securities laws by offering and selling these crypto asset securities to the public in an unregistered offering that was not otherwise exempt from registration.[lxxxii]
Impact Theory agreed to a cease-and-desist order finding that it violated registration provisions of the Securities Act and ordering it to pay a combined total of more than $6.1 million in disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and a civil penalty.[lxxxiii]  The order also established a Fair Fund to return monies that injured investors paid to purchase the NFTs.[lxxxiv]  Impact Theory agreed to destroy all Founder’s Keys in its possession or control, publish notice of the order on its websites and social media channels, and eliminate any royalty that Impact Theory might otherwise receive from future secondary market transactions involving the Founder’s Keys.[lxxxv]
The SEC has also brought enforcement actions against the leading operators of platforms that facilitate the trading of digital assets and that host digital asset wallets.
BINANCE
On June 5, 2023, the SEC charged Binance (which operates the largest digital asset trading platform in the world, Binance.com), U.S.-based affiliate, BAM Trading Services Inc. (which, together with Binance, operates the U.S.-based crypto trading platform, Binance.US), and its founder Changpeng Zhao, with numerous securities law violations.[lxxxvi]  In its complaint, the SEC alleged that although Zhao and Binance publicly claimed that U.S. customers were restricted from transacting on Binance.com, Zhao and Binance “subverted their own [risk management and corporate governance] controls to allow high net worth U.S. customers to continue trading on the Binance.com platform.”[lxxxvii]  The SEC alleged that defendants unlawfully solicited U.S. investors to buy, sell, and trade digital asset securities through unregistered trading platforms available online at Binance.com.[lxxxviii]  The SEC also claims that defendants engaged in unregistered offers and sales of digital asset securities.[lxxxix]  Finally, the SEC alleges that BAM Trading and BAM Management defrauded equity, retail, and institutional investors about purported surveillance and controls over manipulative trading on the Binance.US platform, which were in fact virtually non-existent.[xc]
On June 28, 2024, Judge Amy Berman Jackson of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, who is the presiding judge in this matter, dealt a blow to Binance, which had asked the court to toss the SEC’s lawsuit that alleges that Binance and its founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao broke securities laws.[xci]  The ruling adds to the digital asset trading platform’s woes after Binance agreed in November to pay $4.3 billion to settle with the Department of Justice[xcii] and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission over illicit finance breaches.[xciii]  The ruling marks a partial victory for the broader cryptocurrency sector as she sided with a previous judge in saying that the SEC had not made its case that secondary sales of Binance’s tokens – sold by sellers other than Binance on trading platforms – were not securities.[xciv]
The SEC plans to amend its ongoing lawsuit against Binance and related entities after a court hearing earlier this month where attorneys raised questions about whether a ruling in the case might affect allegations about certain tokens.[xcv]  The SEC has informed defendants, Binance and affiliated entities (namely Binance.US and founder Changpeng Zhao), that it “intends to seek leave to amend its complaint, including with respect to the “Third Party Crypto Asset Securities … obviating the need for the Court to issue a ruling as to the sufficiency of the allegations as to those tokens at this time.”[xcvi]
The issue of third-party tokens came to a head in a hearing on July 9 when attorneys for Binance said they interpreted Judge Jackson’s June 28 ruling on Binance’s motion to dismiss the SEC’s case as moving third-party tokens out of the case.  The judge made it clear that this was not her intention.  Third-party tokens are digital assets issued by various companies apart from Binance that were listed by the crypto exchange.  The SEC alleged that the tokens in the complaint are unregistered securities.
COINBASE
Following the complaint against Binance, the SEC, on the next day, charged Coinbase with operating its crypto trading platform as an unregistered national securities exchange, broker, and clearing agency.[xcvii]  According to the SEC’s complaint, Coinbase has made billions since 2019 by unlawfully facilitating the buying and selling of crypto asset securities.[xcviii]  The complaint alleges that Coinbase (i) provided a marketplace that matches multiple buyers and sellers using non-discretionary methods (i.e., using technology), (ii) facilitated securities transactions for its customers, (iii) provided securities depository services, and (iv) engaged in unregistered securities offerings through its staking-as-a-service program.[xcix]
Of particular interest in the Coinbase complaint is the identification of numerous digital assets that the SEC has identified as securities.[c]  Among those identified were Cardano, Solana, and Polygon, which were among the 10 largest digital assets by market cap in the world.[ci]  The case is also one of the first SEC enforcement actions to allege that the platform acted as an unregistering clearing agency.
On March 27, 2024, Judge Katherine Polk Failla, the judge presiding in the SEC action against Coinbase, ruled that the SEC brought enough of a case arguing that Coinbase is operating as an unregistered broker, exchange, and clearinghouse that its suit against the cryptocurrency company should move forward.[cii]  Judge Failla ruled against most of Coinbase’s motion to dismiss the SEC lawsuit, finding that the regulatory agency had a “plausible” case against the exchange.[ciii]
While the judge said the SEC seemed to have an argument that some of the tokens listed on Wallet might meet the standards for “investment contracts,” Coinbase did not seem to be acting as a brokerage, dismissing that part of the suit.  The other aspects of the suit can proceed, Judge Failla ruled, dismissing claims that the SEC is violating the Major Questions Doctrine (a U.S. Supreme Court ruling prohibiting federal agencies from exceeding their congressional mandates) or the APA.[civ]  Citing the DAO Report, Judge Failla concluded that Coinbase had ample notice that the SEC was pursuing enforcement actions against crypto companies.[cv]
The judge noted, “[w]hen a customer purchases a token on Coinbase’s platform, she is not just purchasing a token, which in and of itself is valueless; rather, she is buying into the token’s digital ecosystem, the growth of which is necessarily tied to value of the token.”[cvi]  Judge Failla stated, “[t]his is evidenced by, among others, the facts that (i) initial coin offerings are engineered to have resale value in the secondary markets, and (ii) crypto-asset issuers continue to publicize their plans to expand and support the token’s blockchain long after its initial offering.”  Finally, the judge concluded, token developers “advertise the fact that capital raised through retail sales of tokens will continue to be re-invested.”[cvii]
CONSENSYS
In June 2024, the SEC charged Consensys Software Inc. (“Consensys”) with engaging in the unregistered offer and sale of securities through the company’s MetaMask Staking service and with operating as an unregistered broker through MetaMask Staking and the company’s MetaMask Swaps service.[cviii]
According to the SEC’s complaint, since at least January 2023, Consensys has offered and sold tens of thousands of unregistered securities on behalf of liquid staking program providers Lido and Rocket Pool, who create and issue liquid staking tokens (called stETH and rETH) in exchange for staked assets.[cix]  While staked tokens are generally locked up and cannot be traded or used while they are staked, liquid staking tokens, as the name implies, can be bought and sold freely.  Investors in these staking programs provided funds to Lido and Rocket Pool in exchange for the liquid tokens.  The SEC’s complaint alleges that Consensys engages in the unregistered offer and sale of securities by participating in the distribution of the staking programs and operates as an unregistered broker with respect to these transactions.
The SEC claims that Consensys has “collect[ed] hundreds of millions of dollars in fees as an unregistered broker and engaging in the unregistered offer and sale of tens of thousands of securities.”[cx]  The SEC also claims that, since at least October 2020, Consensys has brokered transactions in crypto asset securities by, for example, soliciting investors to trade crypto asset securities, providing pricing and other investment information regarding crypto asset securities, purporting to provide investors with the “best” quote, accepting and routing customer orders, facilitating order execution, handling customer assets, and receiving transaction-based compensation.[cxi]  The SEC’s complaint charges Consensys with violating the registration provisions of the Securities Act and the Exchange Act and seeks injunctive relief and penalties.[cxii]
MANN AND FRYE V. SEC
In July 2024, Jonathan Mann and Brian Frye filed suit against the SEC challenging the SEC’s decision to classify NFTs as securities, arguing that this classification limits artistic freedom and creates unnecessary hurdles for digital artists.[cxiii]  Mann and Frye argue that digital art sold as NFTs should not be treated as securities[cxiv] and challenge the SEC’s application of the Howey test to NFTs.  Mann and Frye claim that the case is meant to protect digital artists’ rights[cxv] and seek a declaratory judgment that a proposed NFT by Frye would not violate Sections 5(a) and (c) of the Securities Act.  They also seek an order from the court enjoining the SEC from bringing an enforcement action against them related to their NFT projects.
Mann and Frye argue that there is no “common enterprise” in an NFT “just because artists can and intend to make more art, increase the value of their art, and/or sell that art to a community of loyal fans.”[cxvi]  They also claim “it cannot be that purchasers have a ‘reasonable expectation of profits based on the managerial efforts of others’ where they are not entitled to any ongoing efforts from the artists, even if they are aware that their favorite artists may continue to produce and sell more art.”[cxvii]  Mann and Frye state “when it comes to an art investment, there are no guarantees, no conditions at all, about what the artist may do.  Fundamentally, investors in art can have no reasonable expectations of the artists, and certainly cannot have comparable expectations as securities investors – even if there is a reasonable belief that the artist will continue to promote her art (both specific artworks, as well as an entire body of art).”[cxviii]
PRIVATE PLAINTIFF ACTIONS AGAINST ISSUERS OF NFTS
To date, there are only two reported civil cases where courts have looked at the question of whether NFTs are securities.  The reported decisions in the two cases were at the motion to dismiss stage and neither case has proceeded to summary judgment where a court could determine based on actual facts whether it believed the NFTs at issue are securities.
DAPPER LABS
On May 12, 2021, a plaintiff sued Dapper Labs, Inc. (“Dapper Labs”), the creator of popular NFT platform NBA Top Shot, in New York state court alleging that Dapper Labs sold unregistered securities (in the form of NFTs that capture video highlights, or “Moments”) through its platform.[cxix]  The case was removed to federal court (Southern District of New York) and plaintiff amended the complaint in late 2021 to, among other things, assert claims on behalf of a putative class of plaintiffs.  Dapper Labs filed a motion to dismiss, arguing that the NFTs were collectibles and that their purchase and sale does not constitute the sale of unregistered securities.  Dapper Labs argued that the NFTs are similar to sports trading cards, which are not securities even though they may have some investment value.  Dapper Labs also argued that the value of the NFTs was not directly tied to Dapper’s profitability, the value of the tokens, or the value of other Dapper NFTs.
The court denied Dapper Labs’ motion in February 2023, noting, however, that it was a “close call and the Court’s decision is narrow” and that “[i]f there is a defining line separating those offerings that are securities from those that are not, whether Moments qualify toes that line intimately.”[cxx]  The court focused on the second and third Howey considerations – whether plaintiffs adequately pled a common enterprise and an expectation of profits derived from the essential entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others.[cxxi]
The court found that plaintiffs adequately pleaded a common enterprise through horizontal commonality.  The court held that plaintiffs adequately pled pooling by alleging that Dapper Labs’ sale of packs of Moments and the transaction fees on the marketplace generated revenue used to support and grow the blockchain, purchasers’ capital was then held by Dapper Labs in Dapper-controlled wallets, and Dapper Labs pooled Moments purchasers’ funds to raise additional capital to ensure that the Flow blockchain does not collapse.[cxxii]
The court found that plaintiffs adequately pleaded that the purchasers’ fortunes were tied to the overall success of Dapper Labs by asserting that Dapper Labs controls the enterprise, Moments can only be sold in the marketplace, which is controlled by Dapper Labs, and cited a Sports Illustrated article explaining that when trading was halted on the marketplace, there was a sharp drop in the prices of Moments.[cxxiii]  With respect to whether there was an expectation of profits derived from the essential entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others, the court found that plaintiffs had adequately pleaded a promise of profits through defendants’ public statements and marketing materials.[cxxiv]  The court pointed to tweets that included rocket ship emojis and money bag emojis and noted that they made it plausible that Dapper Labs objectively led purchasers to expect that they would realize the same gains.[cxxv]  With respect to whether the promise was derived from the entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others, the court found that it was plausible that Moments’ value was derived almost entirely from the continued operation by Dapper Labs of the Flow blockchain, which enabled price transparency, but also appeared to provide purchasers with the ability to trade.[cxxvi]
The parties recently entered into a settlement whereby the claims were settled with no admission of liability for $4 million.  As is typical with settlements in civil litigation, the settlement does not address whether the NFTs were securities, but notes that Dapper Labs has made and will make business changes.[cxxvii]
DRAFTKINGS
In March 2023, a purchaser of DraftKings NFTs brought a putative class action lawsuit in federal court in Massachusetts against DraftKings, its CEO and Chairman of the Board, its CFO, and its President on behalf of all persons who purchased or otherwise acquired DraftKings NFTs, alleging that the NFTs are unregistered securities and that defendants were operating an unregistered securities exchange.[cxxviii]  Plaintiff alleged that he purchased $72,263 of DraftKings NFTs on the DraftKings marketplace and sold certain of the NFTs at a loss on the DraftKings secondary market exchange and that his losses exceeded $14,000.[cxxix]  Plaintiff alleged that the NFTs are securities because they constitute investment contracts under Howey.[cxxx]  Defendants filed a motion to dismiss the claims in September 2023, arguing that the NFTs are not securities because they are not investment contracts.
On July 2, 2024, the court denied DraftKings’ motion to dismiss.[cxxxi]  The court went through the Howey test and noted that only the second and third prongs of the test were at issue in the motion – namely whether plaintiff and other purchasers were investing in a common enterprise with the expectation of profits derived solely from the efforts of others.[cxxxii]  The court noted that both parties cited the Dapper Labs decision as the leading case on whether NFTs can be considered a security.[cxxxiii]  In analyzing whether there was a common enterprise, the court concluded that plaintiff had sufficiently alleged that there was horizontal commonality.  The court found that plaintiff had sufficiently alleged the pooling of assets requirement by alleging that the revenue generated by the sale of NFTs was reinvested into DraftKings’ business, including through the promotion of the marketplace,[cxxxiv] and that the pooling resulted in all investors sharing in the risks and profits because the NFTs are sold or traded in the marketplace controlled by DraftKings and if DraftKings shut down the marketplace, the value of the NFTs would plausibly drop to zero.[cxxxv]
With respect to the third element of the Howey test – reasonable expectation of profit from the efforts of others – plaintiff argued that the value of existing NFTs is driven upwards if DraftKings maintains investor interest and demand in the marketplace (a capital appreciation theory).[cxxxvi]  The court noted that: defendants used Twitter to share news on “the biggest risers and fallers” within the NFT marketplace, which had the potential to encourage its audience to view the NFTs as investment opportunities that could be expected to appreciate; certain defendants made statements in a chatroom regarding the profitmaking potential of NFTs; defendants hosted podcasts where NFTs were referred to as investments; and plaintiff alleged that the public viewed DraftKings NFTs as an investment and purchased them with that intent.[cxxxvii]  With respect to whether the profit was solely from the efforts of others, the court found that it was plausible that the NFTs’ values were dependent on the success of the DraftKings marketplace.[cxxxviii]
Four weeks after the court’s decision on defendants’ motion to dismiss, on July 30, 2024, DraftKings announced that it was shutting down its NFT marketplace as well as its first NFT-based fantasy football game due to “recent legal developments.”[cxxxix]
PETITION FOR RULEMAKING
In April 2021, Arkonis filed a petition with the SEC asking the agency to provide regulatory clarity with respect to the regulation of NFTs.[cxl]  Arkonis stated it believed that: (i) in certain instances, NFTs may be securities; (ii) existing securities laws that were written in the 1930s provide a crude mechanism for the regulation of NFTs; (iii) if an NFT relates to an existing asset and is marketed as a collectible with a public assurance of authenticity on the blockchain, it should not be deemed a security; (iv) if an NFT promises a return on investment from the efforts of others, the NFT could be deemed a security; and (v) as noted by the SEC staff in its 2019 Framework, “Price appreciation resulting solely from external market forces (such as general inflationary trends or the economy) impacting the supply and demand for an underlying asset generally is not considered ‘profit’ under the Howey test.’”[cxli]  Arkonis also noted that “[a]s NFTs proliferate, new regulatory questions will arise.”[cxlii]  Arkonis acknowledged that “fractionalized NFTs could be considered a security.  While NFTs are meant to be non-fungible, fractional NFTs that allow numerous purchasers to acquire a partial ownership interest in the NFT increases the likelihood the NFT could be deemed a security.”[cxliii]
Arkonis encouraged the SEC to engage in a meaningful discussion of how to regulate FinTech companies and individuals that are creating NFTs that may be deemed digital asset securities and the platforms that facilitate the issuance and trading of NFTs.[cxliv]  Arkonis also asked the SEC to provide guidance on fractional ownership of an NFT.[cxlv]  Finally, Arkonis “encourage[d] the SEC to publish a concept release on the regulation of NFTs to provide suitable guidance to the industry followed by the adoption of a new regulation on the same.”[cxlvi]
RULEMAKING AND THE APA
As demonstrated by the uncertainty reflected in these recent settlements and lawsuits, rulemaking by the SEC, paired with the required opportunity for public comment, will help alleviate the challenges currently faced by the SEC and the FinTech industry with respect to the proper approach to the regulation of digital assets.  Rulemaking will provide needed guidance to the industry and the public.  By allowing industry participants and the public to raise questions and concerns through rulemaking, the SEC will be able to make a general assessment of the needs of the firms being regulated and to develop a regulatory framework that is better suited to address them.
Rather than publish a concept release or proposed rules on the regulation of digital assets, the SEC has engaged in enforcement actions against FinTech firms that may not have known they were operating in contravention of existing statutes.  The lack of regulatory clarity has left FinTech firms with the choice of seeking no-action relief from the SEC staff.
The regulation of digital assets presents the SEC with an opportunity to satisfy its statutory duties – protecting investors, maintaining fair, orderly, and efficient markets, and facilitating capital formation – by engaging in a constructive dialogue with the FinTech industry on how to regulate digital assets.
While SEC enforcement actions have provided some guidance on when digital assets are securities, the actions have not addressed the needs of FinTech companies dealing with NFTs.  As the SEC routinely notes in guidance to the industry, whether a digital asset is a security depends on the particular facts and circumstances.  Unfortunately, this facts and circumstances approach reserves ultimate discretion to the SEC staff who get to evaluate the facts and circumstances, and the industry is left with the choice of either fighting the SEC or accepting a settlement that may have long-term deleterious consequences for the company and its principals.
The publication of a concept release on how to regulate digital assets and other digital assets would be a meaningful first step in providing guidance to the industry, which would only prove beneficial if it is followed by the SEC adopting a new rule on the regulation of digital assets.  The current guidance on the regulation of digital assets as securities requires a facts and circumstances-based analysis by qualified counsel to determine whether an asset is a security and whether a firm’s activities require registration as a broker-dealer, an exchange, or an ATS.  Such analysis is often cost prohibitive to the early-stage companies that drive much of the innovation in FinTech.  Rulemaking by the SEC will provide much needed guidance to the industry that will promote innovation, market integrity, capital formation, and the protection of investors.
FinTech is revolutionizing the financial services industry with the development of new and innovative digital assets and the facilitation of the trading, clearance, and settlement of those assets.  In many cases, such assets function as traditional securities using new technology and do not fit clearly under the existing regulatory framework.  The pace of change must be tempered by the statutory duties of the SEC to protect investors, maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets, and facilitate capital formation.  To help promote stability and innovation in the industry, the SEC should publish a concept release on the regulation of FinTech, outlining when a digital asset is a security, and what type of registration is required by firms facilitating the trading of digital assets.
CONCLUSION
While many in Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and the arts, sports, and entertainment industries believe in the potential of digital assets, regulators will likely continue to view digital assets with a degree of skepticism.  The most pro-crypto member of the SEC, Commissioner Hester Peirce, has warned the NFT community that fractionalized NFTs could be deemed a security.  Other SEC Commissioners, including Chairman Gary Gensler, have indicated that other digital assets, including Ethereum, were illegally offered securities.  It is unlikely that Chairman Gensler and other SEC Commissioners will take a less expansive approach to the regulation of NFTs and digital assets.  The two civil court decisions on whether NFTs are securities have not been NFT friendly, but neither of those decisions concluded that NFTs were securities; the courts merely denied defendants’ motions to dismiss the claims.  While the SEC may take some confidence from those decisions, ultimately they are of limited precedential value.
While the technology is not fully mature, digital assets represent an attractive option for owners of distinct intellectual property to monetize their property.  However, there are regulatory barriers to widespread adoption of the technology.  Before digital assets can be widely adopted with a degree of confidence, it is imperative that regulators in the United States, Europe, and Asia provide meaningful guidance to the industry on the legal status of digital assets and whether platforms that host the sale and secondary trading of digital assets are required to register as broker-dealers, ATSs, or exchanges.  The FinTech community will have to wait to see who wins the Battle for the Planet of the Bored Apes – the SEC or the FinTech community.

title: Blockchain & Cryptocurrency Laws and Regulations 2025/DIGITAL ASSET LITIGATION DEFENCE: LEVERAGING THE STATUTORY SELLER REQUIREMENT
content:
BLOCKCHAIN & CRYPTOCURRENCY LAWS AND REGULATIONS 2025
DIGITAL ASSET LITIGATION DEFENCE: LEVERAGING THE STATUTORY SELLER REQUIREMENT
FREE ONLINE ACCESS
CHAPTER CONTENT
Background on Section 5, Section 12, and Pinter
The application of the statutory seller requirement to the digital asset industry
Conclusion
The United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under the leadership of Chair Gary Gensler has aggressively pursued enforcement actions against the digital asset industry.[i]  Chair Gensler maintains that “the vast majority of crypto assets” are securities.[ii]  This has translated into an enforcement agenda that has set its sights on many of the projects behind these digital assets.  The SEC plainly believes that many of these issuers have engaged in unregistered securities offerings under Section 5 of the Securities Act.[iii]  The agency also believes that the digital asset intermediaries on which these assets change hands are acting as unregistered exchanges, broker-dealers, and/or clearing agents under the Securities Exchange Act.[iv]  Through enforcement, the SEC has shut down or is attempting to shut down a number of these purported issuers and intermediaries, though it has suffered some notable setbacks.[v]
It has been widely speculated that the upcoming U.S. presidential election could lead to a shift in the SEC’s enforcement priorities no matter which party occupies the White House, including as to the future of digital asset enforcement.[vi]  But even if the SEC shifts away from prioritising digital asset enforcement actions, private plaintiffs will undoubtedly seek to build on the developing case law to continue to attack crypto industry participants.  Over the last several years, plaintiffs’ firms have become increasingly sophisticated about the digital asset industry and have increased their activity in this space.[vii]
In particular, private plaintiffs have relied on Section 12 of the Securities Act, which provides a private right of action to enforce Section 5 of the Securities Act.[viii]  This private right of action under Section 12 is, however, narrower than Section 5 in several key respects, including a shorter one-year statute of limitations, a strict three-year statute of repose, and limitations on secondary liability and available remedies.[ix]  Most significantly, the private right of action imposes a “statutory seller” requirement; that is, the Securities Act provides that recovery is only available “to the person purchasing such security from [the defendant]”.[x]  Under the Supreme Court’s decision in Pinter v. Dahl, only two types of defendants may be held liable as statutory sellers: direct sellers and direct solicitors of plaintiffs’ purchases.[xi]
This chapter focuses on the application of the statutory seller defence to the digital asset industry.  It begins by introducing the legal basis for the statutory seller defence, focusing in particular on recent developments around the solicitation element.  It then discusses the application of this defence to the digital asset industry, including how it has been used by alleged issuers, exchanges, and investors to dismiss claims at the pleading stage of litigation.
BACKGROUND ON SECTION 5, SECTION 12, AND PINTER
Section 5 of the Securities Act prohibits unregistered securities offerings.  Section 5(a) makes it unlawful to sell an unregistered security “through the use or medium of any prospectus or otherwise” “[u]nless a registration statement is in effect”.  Section 5(c) makes it unlawful “to offer to sell or offer to buy through the use or medium of any prospectus or otherwise any security, unless a registration statement has been filed as to such security”.[xii]  Section 4 of the Securities Act provides a number of exemptions from liability under Section 5, including under Section 4(a)(1) for “transactions by any person other than an issuer, underwriter, or dealer”, and under Section 4(a)(2) for “transactions by an issuer not involving any public offering”.
While Section 5 can only be enforced by the government, Section 12(a)(1) provides a narrower private right of action for Section 5 violations[xiii] and permits rescission damages for private plaintiffs.  The SEC can bring Section 5 claims against anyone who sells or offers unregistered securities, but the private right of action under Section 12 is limited to “statutory sellers”.[xiv]  The Supreme Court in Pinter defined statutory sellers as (1) “persons who pass title”, or (2) “the person who successfully solicits the purchase, motivated at least in part by a desire to serve his own financial interests or those of the securities owner”.[xv]  This narrower definition of who may be sued under Section 12 as opposed to under Section 5 derives from the statutory language of Section 12, which only provides a private cause of action against a “person who . . . offers or sells a security in violation of [Section 5]” “to the person purchasing such security from him”.[xvi]  Pinter explained that “the language of [§ 12(a)(1)] contemplates a buyer-seller relationship not unlike traditional contractual privity”.[xvii]  As such, Section 12(a)(1) “imposes liability on only the buyer’s immediate seller” and not “remote sellers”.[xviii]  Pinter also characterised the nature of “solicitation” as being “directed at producing the sale” to the buyer.[xix]
Courts interpreting Pinter have further defined the contours of what it means to be a direct seller or direct solicitor.  The former is more straightforward, while the latter varies more by circuit.
DIRECT SELLER
Pinter held that Section 12 liability attaches “only [to] the buyer’s immediate seller”.[xx]  Courts interpreting Pinter have therefore dismissed Section 12 claims where the defendants are not plausibly alleged to have passed title directly to plaintiffs, including where securities passed through an underwriter before being sold to the ultimate purchasers.[xxi]  In the digital asset context, the direct seller prong of Pinter would typically preclude recovery by purchasers for any sales in the secondary market or on digital asset trading platforms, unless the purchasers bought directly from an issuer, underwriter, or dealer and seek recovery only against that seller.  Given that sales on digital asset trading platforms are typically anonymous, private plaintiffs may frequently face difficulties in identifying direct sellers for these secondary market sales.[xxii]
DIRECT SOLICITOR
Following Pinter, courts have required “direct and active participation in the solicitation of the immediate sale” to meet the solicitation prong.[xxiii]  This standard was clearly articulated by then-Judge Alito in Westinghouse, where he explained that “direct and active participation in the solicitation of the immediate sale is necessary for solicitation liability . . . so as to ensure a direct relationship between the purchaser and the defendant, without which a defendant is simply not a statutory seller”.[xxiv]
The Fifth Circuit agreed with the Third Circuit’s approach, explaining that anything short of direct and active solicitation would allow the plaintiff to leapfrog over his actual seller and go after his seller’s seller, in contravention of Pinter.  The Fifth Circuit explained that “there are unusual cases in which the issuer is sufficiently active in promoting the securities as to essentially become the vendor’s agent”.[xxv]  But it went on to explain that the “usual” case involves “preparing a prospectus and conducting a road show” and suggested that more was needed for an issuer to solicit the sale under Pinter.[xxvi]  The Second Circuit took a similar approach in Capri v. Murphy.[xxvii]  The court there denied a motion to dismiss as to two defendants who actually “prepared and circulated the prospectus to plaintiffs”, but dismissed the solicitation claims against a different defendant who never “actually solicited their investment”.[xxviii]  The Tenth Circuit has ruled that merely alleging that a defendant “induced” a purchase is not sufficient, and that an allegation of “direct and active solicitation” is required.[xxix]
Courts applying the “direct and active” solicitation standard have typically required direct contact between the seller and purchaser in the context of a specific, contemplated transaction.  For example, the court in Gas Reclamation, Inc. Securities Litigation credited evidence that the defendant’s agent prepared the relevant prospectuses, but nonetheless granted summary judgment in the defendant’s favour on the Section 12 claim because “there [was] no evidence of direct contact between [the defendant’s agent] and any of the investors”.[xxx]  Similarly, the court in In re Newbridge Networks Sec. Litig. held that “absent any allegation of direct contact of any kind between defendants and plaintiff-purchasers, the Court rules as a matter of law that defendants are not statutory sellers”.[xxxi]
Several courts have further required the defendant to urge or persuade the purchaser to buy the alleged securities.  For example, in Ryder Int’l Corp. v. First Am. Nat. Bank, the court held that there was no solicitation where the purported solicitor did not persuade the purchaser to buy securities.[xxxii]  In that case, the defendant provided rates on commercial paper in response to inquiries from the plaintiff purchaser and executed transactions on its behalf, but did not actively reach out to the purchaser.  Similarly, in VT Investors v. R & D Funding Corp., the court held that there was no solicitation where “[t]here is no mention of urging, or persuasion, words used by the Supreme Court in Pinter to describe the act of solicitation”.[xxxiii]
In the same vein, courts have held that general public statements alone are not sufficient to constitute solicitation.  For example, the court in Marriott rejected the argument that “defendants ‘solicited’ the plaintiffs’ open market purchases of Marriott notes because defendants made public statements upon which the PPM plaintiffs relied in deciding whether or not to purchase Marriott notes in the open market”.[xxxiv]  Turning to the question of whether purchasers in Marriott’s firm commitment offering were solicited, the court explained that “[t]o find ‘solicitation’ in a case in which no attempt has been made by a defendant to channel information to the particular plaintiff would result in the broadening of the definition of a statutory ‘seller’ to such an extent as to render meaningless the Supreme Court’s statement that ‘a buyer cannot recover against his seller’s seller’”.[xxxv]
Two Circuits, however, have recently expanded the meaning of solicitation in the age of social media and electronic communications.  The Eleventh Circuit recently held that online promoters of a cryptocurrency could be held liable as sellers under Section 12 even without directly contacting the plaintiffs.[xxxvi]  The promoter in that case created thousands of online videos extolling the cryptocurrency that were viewed millions of times.  The district court dismissed the solicitation claims against the promoters because they did not directly solicit each plaintiff, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed and held that generally available promotional statements can constitute solicitation.  The court was of the view that “[Pinter] says nothing about what solicitation entails” and instead relied on the plain meaning of “solicitation”.[xxxvii]
The Ninth Circuit recently followed suit and held that advertisements on social media may be sufficient to constitute solicitation.[xxxviii]  The Ninth Circuit’s decision followed the Eleventh Circuit’s decision in BitConnect and relied on the meaning of “offer”, without addressing the “purchase” limitation found in Section 12.  When confronting the Supreme Court’s statement in Pinter that “the language of [Section 12(a)(1)] contemplates a buyer-seller relationship not unlike traditional contractual privity”, the Ninth Circuit reasoned that the Supreme Court did not intend to require literal privity to find solicitation, since Pinter had also held that selling extends beyond passing title.[xxxix]
Both circuit decisions were also decided against the backdrop of a rapidly changing modern communications landscape different from the one familiar to the drafters of the Securities Act nearly 90 years ago and Pinter more than 35 years ago.  Courts are divided on whether this evolution should influence their understanding of solicitation in the modern, digital asset context.  For example, in Risley v. Universal Navigation Inc., which included Section 12 claims against the decentralised finance (DeFi) exchange[xl] Uniswap and its investors, the court held that certain tweets by defendants did not amount to the required direct solicitation, and that “[t]here is simply no intellectually honest way to read Section 12(a)(1) in a manner that allows the Court to reach Plaintiffs’ requested outcome”.[xli]  By contrast, in Combs v. SafeMoon LLC, involving Section 12 claims against entities and individuals that launched the SafeMoon token, the court held that “the statute simply does not support a directness requirement”, and liability as a solicitor can be based on “mass communications disseminated through social media platforms”.[xlii]
Courts are divided on this question, but the weight of authority remains in favour of a direct and active solicitation requirement, with at least four Circuits (the Second, Third, Fifth, and Tenth) supporting this position, with only two Circuits (the Ninth and Eleventh) holding that mass communications can support solicitation.[xliii]
THE APPLICATION OF THE STATUTORY SELLER REQUIREMENT TO THE DIGITAL ASSET INDUSTRY
Many defendants in the digital asset industry have successfully used the statutory seller defence to win dismissal of Section 12 claims at the pleading stage.  Given that the typical class action plaintiff purchased anonymously on a digital asset trading platform, relatively few plaintiffs even attempt to argue that defendants were direct sellers.  The key issue therefore is often whether plaintiffs adequately pleaded solicitation, which a variety of industry participants – including alleged issuers, platforms, and investors – have litigated to varying outcomes.
ISSUERS
Putative class action plaintiffs often try to pursue alleged issuers of digital assets for secondary market sales in which the issuer does not pass title to the digital asset.  In these circumstances, plaintiffs may try to rely on white papers or other generic marketing materials or promotional statements made by alleged issuers and their principals to support their direct solicitation arguments.  For example, in Holsworth v. BProtocol, purchasers of a digital asset created by a Swiss foundation sued the alleged issuer under Section 12 for failing to register its digital asset.  The purchasers did not purchase from the defendant, so they only alleged that they were solicited by the foundation to purchase on secondary market platforms through various public marketing materials.  The court dismissed the suit on multiple grounds, including that plaintiffs failed to plead any direct contact by defendants or that they purchased securities as a result of any active solicitations by defendants.[xliv]
DIGITAL ASSET TRADING PLATFORMS
Purchasers of digital assets have also tried to bring claims against digital asset trading platforms that they allege list unregistered securities.  The SEC may bring actions against digital asset trading platforms on the basis that they are alleged unregistered national securities exchanges under Section 5 of the Exchange Act,[xlv] but there is no private right of action for this provision.[xlvi]  Private plaintiffs have therefore instead tried to bring Section 12 claims against digital asset platforms, but platforms typically match customer counterparties to sales rather than engage directly in sales to customers, and therefore do not directly pass title to purchasers.  DeFi platforms are likely to have particularly strong arguments along these lines.[xlvii]
The Second Circuit’s recent decision in Oberlander v. Coinbase highlights some of the key issues likely to arise in Section 12 cases against trading platforms.[xlviii]  In Coinbase, the district court rejected arguments under both prongs of Pinter, holding that title never passed to the platform so it was not a direct seller and that the defendant’s public promotion of cryptocurrency was more akin to “marketing efforts” rather than the required “active solicitation”.[xlix]  The Second Circuit reversed, noting that plaintiffs had adequately pleaded that Coinbase passed title to the digital assets based on language in its user agreement describing it as the seller.[l]  The Second Circuit therefore did not reach the solicitation prong of Pinter.
In Risley, the court dismissed Section 12 claims against a DeFi trading platform.  The plaintiffs argued that they met the direct seller prong because the defendants wrote the contracts underlying every sale on the platform.  The court rejected this argument, holding that the defendants never held title to the digital assets traded on the platform, nor did they control the platform.[li]  The court also rejected the plaintiffs’ solicitation argument because their allegations were conclusory, did not plead successful solicitation, and did not amount to direct and actual solicitation.[lii]
INVESTORS
Finally, investors in the issuers of digital assets such as venture capital firms may be the subject of Section 12 litigation.  Because there is no private cause of action for aiding and abetting the issuer’s Section 5 violation, the primary avenue for plaintiffs to pursue liability against investors in alleged issuers is often to allege that the investors solicited an unregistered sale.  In Ocampo v. Dfinity, the state court applying Section 12 held that the plaintiff failed to adequately plead solicitation by a venture capital fund that had invested in a purported issuer of digital assets absent direct and immediate solicitation.[liii]  However, in Houghton v. Leshner, purchasers of COMP tokens alleged that they were solicited by investors in a purported decentralised autonomous organisation, including by alleging that the defendants took part in the “design and governance” of the token.  The court declined to dismiss the complaint under the Ninth Circuit’s solicitation standard and held that allegations concerning the defendants’ “hands-on roles with development of crypto assets in general and COMP in particular” were sufficient to survive the motion to dismiss.[liv]
CONCLUSION
The statutory seller defence is an effective tool for defeating certain private securities claims at the pleading stage, particularly where the plaintiff cannot allege that the defendant passed title directly to him, such as in a secondary market transaction on a digital asset trading platform.  While there is a split in authority on what is sufficient to constitute solicitation under Section 12, most courts have held that there must be direct contact between the defendant and plaintiff.  And in any circuit, alleged solicitation statements must urge a plaintiff to purchase, not merely provide information about a project.  The law will continue to develop and mature in this space, and there should be even more clarity and uniformity as to where this line is drawn.
