title: Blockchain & Cryptocurrency Laws and Regulations 2025/ACCOUNTING CONSIDERATIONS FOR CRYPTOASSETS
content:
BLOCKCHAIN & CRYPTOCURRENCY LAWS AND REGULATIONS 2025
ACCOUNTING CONSIDERATIONS FOR CRYPTOASSETS
FREE ONLINE ACCESS
CHAPTER CONTENT
Abstract
Overview
Staking
Proof-of-reserves
Stablecoin reporting
Summary and conclusions
ABSTRACT
This chapter will discuss and present several of the major accounting and financial reporting issues that continue to face the accounting blockchain and tokenised asset space.  While bitcoin and other cryptoassets have rapidly moved from the fringe of financial services to mainstream financial instruments issued and governed by some of the largest financial institutions, the accounting, attestation and reporting arrangements surrounding these cryptoassets remain very much a work in progress.  In addition to discussing the importance of accounting for cryptoassets as it pertains to financial markets and reporting, this chapter will also present and examine several of the more topical issues facing the accounting profession, including accounting for staking, proof-of-reserves (PoR), and how to integrate stablecoins into accounting guidelines.
OVERVIEW
Cryptoassets have had a volatile time in the public markets ever since bitcoin burst into the mainstream conversation in 2017.  Following that dramatic run-up, where bitcoin hit the first of several all-time highs of approximately $20,000, the mainstream investment and asset management world became aware of the asset for the first time.  Following this initial surge of interest, the subsequent collapse in prices during the bear market of 2018–2019, and the recovery that persisted into 2024, much has changed as it relates to the industry.  What began as a means of disintermediating financial institutions and creating a parallel financial ecosystem and payment network has morphed into an asset class embraced by many of the largest TradFi (traditional finance) institutions in the world.  One aspect that has remained relatively slow to evolve is the accounting and auditing rules for cryptoassets, and this continues to serve as an obstacle for organisations seeking to enter the space.
Given the numerous legal conversations, and the analysis that has been performed in real time in the aftermath of the collapse of FTX, the accounting and auditing conversations might seem like a lesser topic to discuss.  Adding to this conversation are the bevy of factors that have emerged as institutional capital continues to flow into the crypto ecosystem via bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), ether ETFs, and tokenisation of real-world assets.  As these institutional products develop and grow, however, addressing the accounting, reporting, and disclosure issues around these instruments is going to increase in priority for regulators and investors.  This is especially true given the conversations and controversy around proposed plans to repay FTX creditors and investors with cryptoassets that have increased substantially in value since the collapse of the exchange (Randles, 2024).  With policymakers on both sides of the political spectrum seemingly embracing crypto in 2024, this might seem like an opportunity for investors and advocates to exhale and look forward with optimism.
The reality is more nuanced, as the lack of crypto-specific accounting rules and/or auditing standards continues to make it difficult for service providers (but especially those based in the U.S.) to offer standardised and consistent services and results for investors and entrepreneurs.  Actions taken in December 2023 by the Financial Accounting Standards Board have partially addressed crypto accounting issues by allowing organisations that hold said assets to mark them to market, which was a long-awaited development.  In fact, speculation has included the fact that the transparency delivered by this proposed accounting standards update (ASU) is so beneficial that organisations might consider early adoption of this rule (Mishler, 2024).  Although this standard, ASU 2023-08, addresses the accounting concerns related to bitcoin and other related assets, several substantial portions of the crypto marketplace remain unaddressed.  Stablecoins, non-fungible tokens, and the entire decentralised finance ecosystem are not covered by either this ASU or other additional authoritative pronouncements.
Several additional problems that have been created due to the lack of authoritative standards include, but are not limited to, the following:
Lack of consistent information. One of the biggest drawbacks associated with the lack of authoritative and consistent reporting standards is the fact that this means that investors and regulators are not working with the same level or types of information.  Accounting information, and more generally speaking financial reporting on a broader basis, is only as valuable as it is useful.  Since large swaths of the cryptoasset economy have been specifically exempted from the crypto accounting standards that have been written, this limits the usefulness of said data, even with the standards that have been issued.
Opportunities for unethical behaviour. The obvious example of crypto fraud and abuse is FTX and the fraudulent activities that have been proven in court, but that is only part of the conversation.  The larger issue that is partially driven by the lack of consistent and standardised reporting and accounting information is that this lack of standards allows a number of options to be put forward as a solution to crypto reporting problems.  Discussed in more detail below, PoR is an idea that presents a solid premise, but is also an idea that misses important information if implemented as currently designed and understood.  Accounting standards do not prevent fraud, and never have; consistent and agreed-upon reporting allows bad actors and other unethical activity to be noticed and caught quickly.
Ambiguous regulatory environment. Another significant issue that can be raised and illustrated by the lack of crypto-specific accounting standards is the uncertain regulatory environment this lack of guidance contributes to, especially in the U.S.  Depending on which aspect of cryptoassets is discussed, there are any number of oversight agencies that can be thought of as the primary regulator.  These include the Internal Revenue Service, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the Commodities and Futures Trading Commission, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and a number of other federal agencies.
Accounting standards and rule-making might not generate the excitement of either the cryptoasset marketplace price swings nor the court cases and motions that dominate crypto headlines, but these standards play an important role in the maturation of cryptoassets and tokenisation at large.  In addition, concerns around interoperability and other technological-related issues continue to pose challenges to both firms and practitioners looking to integrate crypto into operations (Vollmer, 2022).  The issues and accounting factors that continue to face the accounting profession seeking to offer services and advice to crypto clients are numerous, but three stand out as both fast-growing and significant, i.e.: staking; improving PoR; and stablecoin reporting.
Before diving into those issues, it seems prudent to level-set some definitions and terminology that will help clarify and distinguish audits services able to be offered by providers, and the limitations therein.
Auditing can be thought of as the most comprehensive service with regard to confirming whether or not the financial information presented is in accordance with the applicable accounting standards.  For U.S. publicly traded organisations, or the U.S. operations of firms located outside of the U.S., this is U.S. GAAP.  Organisations outside of the U.S. tend to utilise International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), but the purpose and intent of the audit is the same.  Upon completion of the engagement, the auditor firm issues an opinion as to the financial statements of the firm.  Note, this opinion does not indicate that the financial statements are completely free of fraud, nor is an unqualified opinion (the highest sought-after opinion) a guarantee of financial success.  Rather, these opinions communicate how closely the financial statements follow the applicable accounting standards.
Let us take a look at a few of the bigger picture issues and items that accounting professionals will need to continue to watch going forward.
STAKING
Staking has rapidly moved from a relatively fringe part of the crypto investing landscape to an area that has continued to be hotly debated by market actors, policymakers, and investors alike.  Prior to diving into some of the implications of the continued rise of staking, let us first revisit the types of staking opportunities that do exist in the marketplace and how these different aspects are differentiated from one another, but in any case represent a convergence of tokenisation, TradFi transactions, and technological advancement (International Financial Law Review, 2023).
PASSIVE STAKING
The most popular type of staking for individuals and institutions that exist in the marketplace is an option that tends to mirror many of the TradFi services options that do exist.  In short, investors deposit tokens/funds either with a centralised exchange or a decentralised exchange that offers staking services, and the investor/depositor receives tokens in return.  Setting aside the tax implications of said policy, which is definitely a hot topic that is worthy of further debate, this does result in cryptoassets being either created or distributed to the investors/depositors that have made funds available to the service offering staking opportunities.
ACTIVE STAKING
More recognisable as a blockchain business/operating activity, an active staking situation would tend to operate in the following manner.  As a sizeable holder and/or investor in the token of a certain exchange or protocol, the staker in question would have a higher probability to be selected as a validator of blocks being added to the previous blockchain-based record.  This process, in turn, helps to create a virtuous cycle by which these larger stakers and/or validators are incentivised to act in a manner that maintains the integrity of the underlying blockchain and does so in an ethical manner to maintain both the network itself and the value of the tokens associated with this blockchain.
Some of the considerations that accompany the rise of staking include, but are not limited to, the following.  Firstly, considering that the offering of staking services tends to be centred around either centralised crypto exchanges or service providers, this does create a centralised risk that has become especially apparent at organisations such as Coinbase, which is publicly traded, undergoes regular audits, and is under constant public scrutiny, and there were questions around just when investors were going to be able to withdraw funds that have been staked.  This was complicated and compounded by the reality that staking rewards were delayed several times, and might have been delayed again according to some reports, which means that these promised returns might not come to market as advertised.  The ongoing legal battle between the SEC and Coinbase continues to illustrate that, even when a regulated entity offers a service, that service itself might be subject to additional questions and scrutiny in the future.
Secondly, trusting these funds and accumulated staking rewards under the protection of a centralised exchange or decentralised protocol also means that there are increased risks for investors seeking to regain more custody and control over this information in the aftermath of the collapse of FTX.  Even if investors are seeking to develop self-custodial services on their own, and possess the technical expertise to do so, this might not be able to be accomplished.  Given that activity on decentralised exchanges moved noticeably upward after the collapse of FTX, and that these activity levels have remained significantly higher than prior to the collapse of FTX, the issues and considerations around staking are not going away.  Specifically, questions around custody, control, and the ability of investors to access funds in the case of bankruptcy or other exigent circumstance continue to remain unaddressed for the most part, which, in the face of more TradFi investing into staking and other crypto activities, are only going to become of more importance moving forward.
The controversy around staking has continued to make headlines, generate debates, and drive conversations in the crypto sector and beyond, and that is only partially due to the tax questions that continue to exist with regard to these offerings.  After the spectacular collapse of FTX, and the ongoing doubts and questions swirling around Binance and other crypto operators, it is not unreasonable to see that regulators are taking a much harder look at how these players operate at large, and not just from a custodial perspective.  Let us take a look at a few of the developments that have occurred and compare what the different types of staking can mean for investors, institutions, and regulators going forward.
WHAT ARE THE ISSUES?
The issues with staking come back to, ultimately, the doubts and questions that investors and regulators alike have with centralised exchanges and operators in the aftermath of a disastrous 2022–2023 for the crypto space.  As a direct result of poor controls, weak governance, and the alleged misappropriation of customer assets, in addition to a market downturn from 2021 to 2022, multiple operators collapsed under the weight of these combined forces.  Staking, by definition, does generate returns (the nature of which is also debated) for the investors, stakers, or depositors that partake in these options.  Despite rising prices and the overall market recovery that has taken place in 2024, the issues and questions that are connected to staking and other crypto-adjacent products/services remain.
Drilling down, the primary questions that arise from this process can be distilled down to one main question: what are the methods by which these returns are generated and/or created?
The most obvious answer, mirroring the TradFi institutions that tend to hold the attention and focus of regulatory agencies, is that in order to generate returns, there are loans and other products created and distributed into the marketplace.  True for the TradFi sector, this does not necessarily mean that similar practices will be carried over on a 1:1 basis in the crypto sector.  Staking, no matter whether it is a passive or active staking arrangement, does involve the creation of new tokens as a result of staking operations, i.e., the validation of blocks as they are added on to the existing blockchain.  Such an arrangement means that, while returns are created, these returns are not always going to be generated via loans or productised operations.  Rather, this value is created as a direct result of the blockchain operating as advertised versus lending out these deposits.
The reluctance that TradFi firms have expressed for offering services to crypto-native organisations, exacerbated by the continued existence of SAB 121 – despite a bipartisan effort to undo it – highlights where accounting rules and emerging crypto services directly overlap.  Even as asset managers have issued multiple bitcoin and ether tradeable products, banking institutions have remained only tangentially involved in tokenisation efforts.  This includes efforts undertaken by organisations such as JP Morgan and SocGen; issuing stablecoins and deploying blockchains for internal purposes do not fully encapsulate the proposed benefits of blockchain technology.  These institutions, however, have been seeking to gain exemptions from the reporting requirements mandated by SAB 121, with announcements in July 2024 indicating these were forthcoming being the only evidence as to the success of these efforts.  As of this writing, however, there have been no public pronouncements regarding the potential exemption of banks and financial institutions from SAB 121 reporting and disclosure requirements.
Alongside ongoing ambiguity as to what services certain institutions can offer, and the roadblocks that have been put in place for financial institutions, one other aspect of crypto accounting and auditing remains an open issue: how can advisors provide any levels of assurance of the information that is reported?  PoR has its advocates and detractors, and has recently been the subject of an updated white paper from the Digital Chamber of Commerce.
PROOF-OF-RESERVES
The idea of PoR has continued to evolve and rotate between being on the front burner and being relegated to the back burner in terms of market attention, development, and regulator attention.  This illustrates the continuing challenge that auditing blockchain-based assets presents for both audit firms and investors that are reliant on audited financial statements (Roberts, 2022).  Specifically in the aftermath of the collapse of FTX, which, in turn, was caused in no small part by the questionable (and ultimately found to be fraudulent) practices at the company, the following question needs to be asked: just how are blockchain and/or crypto organisations going to be audited and examined going forward?  Despite the attention that reserve and solvency engagements have attracted, it is worth pointing out that several accounting firms that were involved in crypto engagements have subsequently withdrawn from the practice area (Nicolle, 2022).
PoR is an idea that, on the surface, represents a definitive step forward in terms of both enabling better reporting for crypto organisations as well as incorporating some of the best accounting and audit standards to this fast-moving space.  Developed with two primary firms in mind – stablecoin issuers and crypto exchanges (such as FTX, Binance, Tether, and Coinbase) – the point of a PoR engagement is to add more transparency and clarity around just what assets actually exist at either a stablecoin issuer or a crypto exchange.  The specifics of every engagement will vary, of course, but it is worth taking a look at some of the commonalities that practitioners need to take into account when assessing (1) how to deploy a PoR type of solution, and (2) what factors need to be included in these types of engagements to make them worthwhile and understandable for investors, users, and regulators alike.
Additional factors related to PoR have to do with how these types of engagements are going to need to update and change the existing audit and attestation processes.  Let us take a look at a few of the primary factors that can connect the PoR engagements and traditional audit structures.  It is also worth pointing out that despite being called an audit by some crypto organisations, these reserve attestation agreements are not audits but do fall on the spectrum of accounting and attestation-related services (Bauer, et al., 2024).
POST-BALANCE SHEET ISSUES
One of the highest-profile issues that has arisen with regard to reserve engagements relates to the questions that have arisen around the potential window-dressing that has occurred around several of the most prominent reserve engagements.  Both Binance and crypto.com have drawn scrutiny for a number of issues as it pertains to financial statements and financial reporting, but one of the most important issues has to do with the movement of funds from off-balance sheet forces to the proper balance sheet of these organisations.  This process, and the implications therein, are well understood by TradFi institutions and investors that rely on financial data provided by them; mainstream media such as CNBC and Bloomberg openly discuss such actions.  When it connects to tokenised assets, however, the discussion is at a much earlier stage and consists of a much smaller population, leading to the possibility of misinterpretation and miscommunicating data to the marketplace.
COMMINGLING FUNDS
One other factor that needs to be assessed is that – at a fundamental level – the internal controls and processes that are well established in the TradFi marketplace do not exist in a codified format for crypto firms.  Specifically, for stablecoin issuers and exchanges, one of the most important factors is that customer and institutional funds must be kept separate, with no cross-access or contamination allowed.  The impact of this has been relatively rapid, with even some of the most conservative instruments not escaping the risks and scrutiny associated with these instruments.  The fact that Coinbase, an SEC registrant and the only publicly traded U.S. crypto exchange, continues to be embroiled in legal arguments with the SEC is a clear sign that even those organisations that were assumed to be offering legitimate and approved services might not be entirely clear of future legal liabilities.
Overall, one of the most glaring issues with regard to reserve engagements is the simple fact that these types of engagements are not accounting standards, nor legal laws, nor widely accepted.  Until these issues have been resolved, it seems apparent that these engagements should be viewed as a worthy step in this process, but are not a final draft at this point in time.  The private sector can certainly, and should always, play an important role in the development of emerging standards, but the responsibility for crafting and developing legislation and rule-making remains with lawmakers or policymakers (Huang, Wang and Yen, 2024).
Other issues that exist as they pertain to PoR is that this attestation is not only not standardised in how it is performed but is not the creation of any authoritative accounting standard-setting body.  This led to multiple organisations – including FTX – claiming that these “audits” had been performed on the books and records of the organisation, whereas, in reality, these procedures are not only not audits but are not the issued standards of any authoritative accounting or regulatory body.  This lack of authority around this procedure led to varying levels of reports being issued by exchanges and platforms such as crypto.com, Binance, Coinbase, Kraken, and multiple others.
STABLECOIN REPORTING
Although stablecoins were purpose built and designed to be used as a medium of exchange, this has not eliminated the accounting questions or issues that these tokenised instruments create.  In short, stablecoins have been specifically designed to combine the best aspects of fiat payment rails and tokenised payment options, but even relatively straightforward stablecoins raise issues for accounting professionals (Gongpil, 2021).  These questions have continued even as firms such as Visa have moved to allocate substantial amounts of capital (financial and intellectual) to develope crypto-adjacent products, including stablecoins (Adams, 2023).  Following the issues, and depegging, that occurred during the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and the USDC token issued by Circle, the importance of stablecoin reporting and disclosures has only become even higher-profile.  As TradFi institutions continue to embrace the opportunities of stablecoins, with PayPal issuing a native stablecoin and SocGen issuing the first freely traded and Euro-backed stablecoin able to be traded by investors, it might be assumed that reporting standards had kept pace.  Despite the rapid foray into stablecoins by multiple crypto-native and TradFi institutions, however, stablecoin reporting and disclosure frameworks have yet to keep pace.  Several of the accounting issues that stablecoins create that are unique to these cryptoassets include the following.
INTERNAL CONTROLS AND GOVERNANCE
Since stablecoins by nature consist of two financial instruments – the underlying reserve asset and the token itself – the internal control processes and structures that surround access and control over both of these assets will only increase in importance as the integration of tokenised payments continues.  In August 2024, Mastercard announced the first-of-its-kind direct partnership with a decentralised finance entity through its debit card launched in conjunction with MetaMask and Baanx.  Building on the suite of products and services that Mastercard offers to existing clients seeking to onboard crypto, the importance of internal controls and trust is self-evident.
Accounting takeaway: do all member firms of the payment network in question have appropriate controls and policies in place to safeguard access to both the underlying reserve assets and tokens themselves?
RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS
Following the collapse of FTX, the subsequent bankruptcy that revealed severe ethical wrongdoings, and the increase in crypto prices that made recovery in excess of 100% possible, the rights of token holders became a front-page issue.  For stablecoins, this question is always present, as the redemption policies of every token issued need to both be understood and factored into the valuation of the coin in question.  For example, USDT (issued by Tether) has long been dogged by questions around the accuracy of Tether’s financial reporting and reserve asset composition.  USDC, issued by Circle, is considered by many to be a better-managed stablecoin.  Interestingly, it was Circle that suffered from the collapse of SVB, due to an excess of $3 billion deposited at the institution that was temporarily unavailable, causing the peg of USDC to break below $1/$1 for a period of time.
Accounting takeaway: are the rights and potential obligations of all stablecoins being used by the client in question understood and clear?  If so, how are these communicated to the investing marketplace, if at all?
In light of these ongoing accounting questions and concerns, the number of TradFi institutions entering the stablecoin space should come as no surprise.  Combining the ongoing questions and uncertainty that some investors have regarding crypto at large and the failure of PoR to assuage such concerns, the reputation and capabilities of larger institutions have been deployed to assist with this integration process.  Specifically, the efforts that have been launched by SocGen, JP Morgan and PayPal to create and issue native stablecoins are indicative of both the demand for stablecoins and the need for more trust and transparency around these financial instruments.  These entrants into the stablecoin space, paradoxical as they might seem at first, are in direct response to the volatility and failures that have occurred to date around these assets.  Specifically, with the vast majority of stablecoins backed on a 1:1 basis by the U.S. dollar, the recent rise in interest by U.S. financial institutions and payment processors in developing stablecoin products can also be seen as a way to upgrade the competitiveness of the dollar moving forward (Greenwald, 2023).  That said, stablecoins continue to have doubters, with notable failures ensuring that questions and fears remain.
One notable example of how stablecoins can fail, and cause a cascading range of failures throughout the wider cryptoasset marketplace, is best exemplified by Terra and the Terra stablecoin.  An organisation headquartered in South Korea, TerraLabs had developed what is known as an algorithmic stablecoin, which is a stablecoin actively managed and governed by a series of smart contracts versus centrally managed governance protocols.  The Terra stablecoin was pegged on a 1:1 basis to the U.S. dollar, and the maintenance of this peg was partially enabled by the Luna governance token, a secondary token also issued by Terra.
Without diving into overly specific minutia, the relationship between the Terra stablecoin and Luna governance token allowed the price peg of the Terra stablecoin to be maintained, while also allowing the valuation of the governance token to fluctuate in response to market demand for both the token and Terra stablecoin.  Adding to the complexity of this situation is the fact that the Terra stablecoin was also an integral component of the Anchor decentralised finance protocol, which promised investors returns of nearly 20%.  Given the reality of low interest rates across the globe, returns of 20% should not have seemed sustainable, and ended up not being so.
In May 2022, the price of bitcoin continued its decline, and with the greater volatility in the cryptoasset marketplace, including a decline in market sentiment and positivity, this caused pressure to grow on Terra.  At a certain point, with this increasing pressure, the organisation filed for bankruptcy protection, leading to further cascading failures and price declines in the wider cryptoasset marketplace.  Given this context, it should come as little surprise that (1) progress on comprehensive stablecoin legislation and rule-making has slowed substantially following 2022, and (2) the flurry of activity among TradFi actors and stablecoins has accelerated following these incidents.  As of this writing, the prospect of a widely available and traded stablecoin issued by a major financial institution remains more a concept than reality, but the geopolitical implications alone will keep policymakers interested for the foreseeable future.
SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
The accounting landscape for cryptoassets continues to be one that is volatile in nature as well as in need of further clarification and rule-making.  No matter what form the final rules and regulations take in terms of the crypto accounting world, the reality is that establishing and maintaining consistent, effective, and useful financial reporting data will continue to be important for the continued growth and adoption of cryptoassets by both individuals and institutions.  Issues around staking of certain tokens, reporting and disclosure pertaining to stablecoins, and the open questions that exist around PoR are just a handful of the accounting-adjacent issues that need to be addressed.  That said, the progress that has been made to date is worth noting, building upon, and working with to ensure continued growth of transparency and trust in the crypto ecosystem.
